newsitem.title: INDIA: Scandal shadows budget debate in India parliament.
newsitem.headline: Scandal shadows budget debate in India parliament.

text.p: India's parliament on Wednesday opened a 2-1/2-week budget session and was quickly engulfed in debate over a corruption scandal plaguing the nine-day-old government.
Hindu nationalists demanded that the leader of Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party step down after being linked to the $280 million corruption case.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, president of Gujral's Janata Dal party and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, has refused to quit his posts despite being the target of a probe by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
His refusal has embarrassed Gujral's party, which is the biggest component of the 15-party United Front coalition.
Lawmakers said the reputation of Gujral, who was sworn in on April 21, as a clean leader was at stake as a result.
"The government will be transparent. There will be no witch-hunting. Anybody who has committed a crime will not be spared. I will only repeat these," Gujral said.

The federal police agency said on Sunday it planned to prosecute Yadav and 55 others in the 10 billion rupee ($280 million) scandal, which stretches back more than a decade but was uncovered only last year.

The CBI said it also intended to prosecute junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma, also a member of the Janata Dal, which has 45 of the United Front's 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house.
Both Yadav and Varma have said they are innocent.
"I want to know if the CBI wants to prosecute Mr Varma, what is the approach of the government?" said Atal Bihari Vajpayee, leader of the opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Vajpayee said the prime minister should not hesitate to force even politicial heavyweights who are implicated in scandals to step down.

The leader of the Congress party in the lower house, Sharad Pawar, said Yadav should quit once the Bihar governor grants permission to the CBI to indict the chief minister. "There should be something to uphold moral responsibility," he said.
The Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), part of the United Front, joined in calls for Yadav's resignation.
"Everybody is innocent until proven guilty but people occupying some positions cannot take that attitude," said CPI-M parliamentary leader Somnath Chatterjee.
The debate on corruption overshadowed pressing financial business that lawmakers have pledged to take care of by May 16, when the session is scheduled to end.

The lower house, the Lok Sabha, was not expected to take up the Finance Bill, the crux of the 1997/98 (April-March) budget package which incorporates proposed tax and tariff cuts, until May 7 and voting was expected on May 9, a parliamentary official said. But he said the dates were yet to be decided.
Gujral's fledgling government received a boost on Tuesday when former finance minister P. Chidambaram's regional party announced it would enter the council of ministers.
Chidambaram, respected in financial markets for his advocacy of free-market reforms, was to return to the cabinet as finance minister, government officials said.

Share prices on the Bombay exchange jumped over one percent in early trade on news that the Tamil Maanila Congress party had decided to enter Gujral's government and Chidambaram would return as finance minister. But profit-taking pared gains and the market ended up a provisional 0.81 percent.
The swearing-in of Chidambaram and up to five other ministers, originally set for 7:30 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Wednesday, was postponed to 6 p.m. (1230 GMT) on Thursday, officials said.
The delay followed a request by the prospective ministers and did not reflect any hitch in the government's plans, an official said.
